I think about how life would have been different if the event had not occurred
Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation

Memory.value: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
When I remember the event I feel intense rage
There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try

I have lost my connection to my community and culture
I have permanently changed for the worse

vignette: Akua had always taken pride in her work as a police officer, patrolling the streets of her predominantly African-American neighborhood with a sense of purpose and responsibility. But on that fateful night two years ago, everything changed. She was working a late shift when she was attacked by a suspect she had been trying to apprehend. The assault left her shaken, both physically and emotionally. In the aftermath of the attack, Akua began to notice changes in herself. Certain situations would trigger intense emotions, making her feel like she was reliving that night all over again. She started avoiding any scenario that might make her feel strong emotions - whether it was a heated argument with her husband or a particularly gruesome crime scene at work. "I just can't handle it," she'd tell herself, feeling overwhelmed by the prospect of confronting her feelings head-on. Akua also found herself increasingly preoccupied with thoughts of how life would have been different if the assault hadn't happened. She'd think about all the what-ifs - what if she had taken a different route home that night? What if she had responded differently to the suspect's advances? "If only..." became her constant refrain, as she replayed the events leading up to the attack over and over in her mind. But it was when memories of the assault itself began to resurface that Akua felt truly overwhelmed. The recollections would come flooding back, accompanied by searing physical pain in the same parts of her body where she'd been injured during the attack. She'd feel intense rage welling up inside her, as if the anger had been simmering just beneath the surface all along. There were times when Akua couldn't remember specific details about that night - memory gaps that left her feeling frustrated and helpless. Akua's negative self-talk began to take on a life of its own. She'd compare herself unfavorably to others, wondering how someone else might have handled the situation differently. "Why didn't I fight back harder?" she'd berate herself. "What was wrong with me that night?" The assault had left her feeling like she'd lost her connection to her community and culture - as if she no longer fit in or belonged. Akua felt like she'd been forever changed by the experience, that some essential part of her had been irreparably damaged. She began to withdraw from social interactions, avoiding friends and family who didn't understand what she was going through. At work, she became increasingly isolated, feeling like a stranger among colleagues who seemed to have moved on with their lives while hers remained stuck in limbo. As the months went by, Akua's relationships began to fray at the edges. Her husband grew tired of her constant mood swings and avoidance behaviors, feeling helpless as he watched his wife retreat further into herself. "I just want my old Akua back," he'd say, exasperated by her lack of emotional availability. It was only when Akua realized she could no longer perform her duties effectively - that the stress and anxiety were starting to affect not just her personal life but also her work as a police officer - that she finally sought help. She knew it wouldn't be easy, that confronting her demons head-on would require a level of courage and vulnerability she wasn't sure she possessed. But Akua also knew she couldn't keep living like this - stuck in the past, unable to move forward or reconnect with the world around her. As she sat in her therapist's office for the first time, nervously clutching her hands together, she felt a glimmer of hope that maybe, just maybe, things could get better.
